question.leadin: Give the following about Spanish Florida.
question.text: The Spanish founded this city in Florida in 1565, making it America's oldest city.
question.clue: The 1763 Treaty of Paris ceded this city's colony, against which James Oglethorpe led a 1740 expedition.

swap.leadin: Answer some questions about the early colonization of New England.
swap.text: This Puritan minister founded Rhode Island after being expelled from Massachusetts. He was one of the first abolitionists and wrote the first book about Native American languages.
swap.clue: Earlier in his life, he chafed at Archbishop William Laud's strict control of Anglican Church doctrine, escaping with his wife Mary to Boston.

question.leadin: This publication predicted the death of Titan Leeds in 1732. Leeds wasn't dead in 1733, but this publication printed an obituary anyway; when Leeds protested, this publication suspected an imposter.
question.text: Name this annual publication, filled with astronomical information, poems, proverbs, and a calendar, that was extremely popular in the American colonies.
question.clue: Naval hero John Paul Jones named his ship after this publication.

swap.text: Originally intended as a fort to protect the Dutch West India Company's fur interests in the area, this settlement was handed over to the British in exchange for a tiny island near Suriname in the Treaty of Breda. This settlement was later renamed New York City.
swap.clue: A fort in this settlement was constructed by what became a non-Ohio Bowling Green.

question.leadin: This man began one speech by quoting the line "their foot shall slide in due time."
question.text: Name this preacher, who compared people to spiders held above a fire in his sermon "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God."
question.clue: This man worked to undo his grandfather Solomon Stoddard's Half-Way Covenant policy, though he inherited Stoddard's land at Northampton.

swap.leadin: Everyone likes pirates! Answer these questions about real pirates.
swap.text: In 1718, this man blockaded the port of Charlestown with his ship The Queen Anne's Revenge and two smaller vessels. He allegedly lit fuses around his face to appear more menacing.
swap.clue: This man used the wealth gained from rogue toll operations in Pamlico Sound to purchase protection from Charles Eden of North Carolina and eventually redubbed the Concorde the Royal James after earlier flying it under the moniker Queen Anne's Revenge.

question.leadin: John Ingram led this rebellion after its namesake leader's death.
question.text: Name this first major rebellion in the American colonies, which was able to successfully send William Berkeley back to England.
question.clue: The leader of one side during this event attempted to ally with Cockacoeske ("ka-ka-ko-ESS-kee"), the "Queen of Pamunkey."

swap.text: Few of these Native people survived into the Dominion eta. This Rhode Island tribe suffered a heavy defeat inthe 1675 Great Swamp Fight after being accused of harboring members of the Wampanoag Tribe.
swap.clue: This tribe's language is the origin of the English words "powwow," "squash," and "papoose," as noted in an early ethnolinguistic study.

question.leadin: Name these conflicts between Native Americans and European settlers.
question.text: When Metacom, the successor of Massasoit, took control of the Wampanoags, he allied with the Narraganset for this 1675 to 1676 conflict with Massachussets settlers.
question.clue: A turning point in this conflict occurred with the Great Swamp Fight, after which the Narragansett were forced to withdraw.

swap.leadin: Some of the participants in this revolt were upset that Catholic priests had destroyed their kivas, or ceremonial pits.
swap.text: Identify this 1680 rebellion led by a man named Pope (po-PAY) in modern day New Mexico.
swap.clue: This conflict witnessed the death of about 900 members of the Acomans.

question.leadin: This man, whose son was the namesake of King Philip's War, was once cured of an illness by Edward Winslow, and he changed his name following a war with the Narragansetts.
question.text: Name this Native American sachem who signed a treaty with the Pilgrims in 1621.
question.clue: This was name adopted by Ousamequin, the Great Sachem and Wampanoag chieftain who negotiated a treaty with the Plymouth colonists to gang up on the Narragansetts.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about U.S. relations with Native Americans.
swap.text: Over a century earlier, this group of western Pennsylvanian frontiersmen got so furious in the face of Pontiac's rebellion that they started massacring the peaceful Susquehannock Indians.
swap.clue: Their first fight was prompted by Matthew Smith's reconnaissance, and Asher Clayton and Lazarus Stewart led their two companies, which were started by Colonel Reverend John Elder.

question.text: The Fundamental Agreement of the New Haven Colony created a court of 16 people with this title, who were "chosen out of the church members." Elected representatives in colonial Virginia also had this title.

swap.leadin: Allegedly, a settler gave a chief of this people a compass when he was about to be executed, which he saw as a peace offering.
swap.text: Name these people from modern-day Virginia. John Smith claimed that these people were about to execute him until the intervention of a member of this group, Pocahontas.
swap.answerHtml: Powhatan people [or Powhatan Confederacy; accept Tsenacommacah; prompt on Algonquian people]

question.text: One of the propaganda highlights of the Long March was the capture of one of these structures in Luding County, Sichuan ("SUCH-wahn"). The Japanese invasion of China proper began with a skirmish at one of these structures in Beijing named after Marco Polo.
question.answerHtml: bridges [or qiao; accept Battle of Luding Bridge; accept Marco Polo Bridge Incident]
question.clue: Suetonius wrote that Caligula rode his horse across a temporary one of these objects made of pontoons, and one of these objects collapsed during a retreat of Maxentius's troops.

swap.leadin: During this war, raiders under Jean-Baptiste Hertel de Rouville ("air-TELL duh roo-VEEL") attacked English forces in Deerfield, Massachusetts, killing four dozen colonists.
swap.text: Name this war named after an English monarch, the American theater of the War of Spanish Succession. During this war, the Wabanaki stopped New England from expanding into Acadia.
swap.answerHtml: Queen Anne’s War [or Third Indian War; or Second Intercolonial War]
swap.clue: During this war, British forces made three attempts, the last of which was successful, to capture the Acadian capital of Port Royal, defended by the Wabanaki Confederacy and France.

question.leadin: Identify these preachers active during the Great Awakening FTPE.
question.text: This priest of Boston's First Church was the staunchest opponent of the Great Awakening and warned against believing itinerant preachers. His most famous sermon was Enthusiasm Described and Cautioned Against.
question.clue: Both Whitefield and Edwards were attacked by this Boston divine, whose 1742 sermon Enthusiasm Described and Cautioned Against saw in the Awakening the legacy of the Munster Anabaptists and Antinomians.

swap.text: This colonial woman kept a copy of Bradford's books with her when she was captured during King Philip's War, which she wrote about in her 1682 bestseller The Sovereignty and Goodness of God.
swap.clue: This colonial woman was captured by Native Americans during King Philip's War. Her captivity narrative includes the death of her six-year-old daughter, Sarah.

question.text: De La Warr left this tyrannical deputy of his in charge of Virginia, and then died on a return voyage trying to replace him. This bad-ass once kidnapped Pocahontas, and later commanded an expedition against the French in Algiers.
question.clue: This military leader abducted Pocahantas and held her captive to negotiate with the Powhatan. He later led raids against Acadia and served as governor of the Virginia Colony.

swap.text: Further anti-Andros activity could be seen in New York, where this German-born colonist led a 1689 revolt which deposed Andros' deputy Francis Nicholson. He was eventually executed in 1691 for treason.
swap.clue: The major accomplishment of his two-year-long regime was calling for an attack on Quebec in the first independent congress of the North American colonies.
